fanoutqa_030227.x:
University of Bath :: Coat of Arms :: chunk_0015
The [College of Arms](/wiki/College_of_Arms "College of Arms") has granted the University the following arms[[84]](#cite_note-90):

Coat of arms of University of Bath

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
|  | Granted  15 November 1966  Crest  On a wreath Or, argent and azure, Out of a mural crown argent, an eagle, wings expanded and inverted, Or, supporting with the dexter claw a key, wards upward and outward, silver.  Escutcheon  Azure, a sword in pale argent, hilt and pommel and quillons Or, the point ensigned by a Watt governor proper, between in fess two heads of Sul Or.  Supporters  On the dexter side a wyvern erect vert charged on the body with mullets, each of six points, Or; and on the sinister side a unicorn sejant erect Or, armed, unguled, crined and tufted sable, charged on the body with mullets of six points vert; the whole upon a compartment of water harry wavy of four argent and azure between two river banks proper, sprouting therefrom roses argent, barbed seeded, slipped and leaved proper.  Motto  Generatim discite cultus.  Symbolism  Sul was a Celtic God identified by the Romans with their own Minerva, and Bath was known as Aquae Sulis. The choice of Sul depicted by a conventional rendering of his head as found carved at Bath is fitting indeed, and it can be distinguished from a sun in splendour by the fact that the face is moustached, and eared, and the hair thereof is entwined with and blends with wavy rays of heat that surround the whole.  A Watt Governor is a device designed in 1788 by James Watt who adapted an older type of governor to control his steam engine where it regulates the admission of steam into the cylinder. It is used here as a symbol for a technical university. |

See also: [Category:Alumni of the University of Bath](/wiki/Category:Alumni_of_the_University_of_Bath "Category:Alumni of the University of Bath")

Dell Streak smartphone

The release of Apple's [iPad](/wiki/IPad "IPad") [tablet computer](/wiki/Tablet_computer "Tablet computer") had a negative impact on Dell and other major PC vendors, as consumers switched away from desktop and laptop PCs. Dell's own mobility division has not managed success with developing smartphones or tablets, whether running Windows or [Android](/wiki/Android_(operating_system) "Android (operating system)").[[72]](#cite_note-72)[[73]](#cite_note-beta.fool-73) The [Dell Streak](/wiki/Dell_Streak "Dell Streak") was a failure commercially and critically due to its outdated OS, numerous bugs, and low resolution screen. *InfoWorld* suggested that Dell and other OEMs saw tablets as a short-term, low-investment opportunity running [Google Android](/wiki/Google_Android "Google Android"), an approach that neglected user interface and failed to gain long term market traction with consumers.[[74]](#cite_note-74)[[75]](#cite_note-75) Dell has responded by pushing higher-end PCs, such as the XPS line of notebooks, which do not compete with the [Apple iPad](/wiki/Apple_iPad "Apple iPad") and [Kindle Fire](/wiki/Kindle_Fire "Kindle Fire") tablets.[[76]](#cite_note-76) The growing popularity of smartphones and tablet computers instead of PCs drove Dell's consumer segment to an operating loss in Q3 2012. In December 2012, Dell suffered its first decline in holiday sales in five years, despite the introduction of [Windows 8](/wiki/Windows_8 "Windows 8").[[77]](#cite_note-77)

In the shrinking PC industry, Dell continued to lose market share, as it dropped below [Lenovo](/wiki/Lenovo "Lenovo") in 2011 to fall to number three in the world. According to Rowling, the idea for Harry Potter and the novel series came to her while she was waiting for a train in 1990. She first conceived of Harry as a "scrawny, black-haired, bespectacled boy" who is unaware that he is a wizard.[[2]](#cite_note-jkrbio-3) While developing ideas for the first book, she decided to make Harry an orphan who attends a boarding school called Hogwarts. She explained in a 1999 interview with *[The Guardian](/wiki/The_Guardian "The Guardian")*: "Harry had to be an orphan—so that he's a free agent, with no fear of letting down his parents, disappointing them ... Then there's the security. Having a child of my own reinforces my belief that children above all want security, and that's what Hogwarts offers Harry."[[3]](#cite_note-carey1999-4)

The death of Rowling's mother in December 1990 inspired her to write Harry as a boy longing for his dead parents. She explained that his anguish became deeper and "much more real" than in earlier drafts of the first book because she related to it herself.[[2]](#cite_note-jkrbio-3) In a 2000 interview, Rowling said that the character [Wart](/wiki/King_Arthur "King Arthur") in [T. H. White](/wiki/T._H._White "T. H. White")'s novel *[The Once and Future King](/wiki/The_Once_and_Future_King "The Once and Future King")* is Harry's "spiritual ancestor".[[4]](#cite_note-Guardian2000-5) Although Rowling gave Harry her own birth date of 31 July, she maintains that he is not directly based on any real-life person. She says that he came "out of a part of [her]".[[5]](#cite_note-Raincoast2001-6)

fanoutqa_016915.t: Dara Torres :: International swimming career :: 1984, 1988 and 1992 Olympics :: chunk_0005
fanoutqa_016915.x:
Dara Torres :: International swimming career :: 1984, 1988 and 1992 Olympics :: chunk_0005
[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/be/Dara_Torres_1984.jpg)](/wiki/File:Dara_Torres_1984.jpg)

Torres in 1984

At the [1984 Summer Olympics](/wiki/1984_Summer_Olympics "1984 Summer Olympics") in Los Angeles, Torres was a member of the winning U.S. women's [4×100-meter freestyle relay](/wiki/Swimming_at_the_1984_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women%27s_4_%C3%97_100_metre_freestyle_relay "Swimming at the 1984 Summer Olympics – Women's 4 × 100 metre freestyle relay") team, swimming in the first-round qualifying heat and earning a gold medal in the event final.[[11]](#cite_note-sroprofile-11) Her winning teammates in that final included [Nancy Hogshead](/wiki/Nancy_Hogshead "Nancy Hogshead"), [Jenna Johnson](/wiki/Jenna_Johnson "Jenna Johnson"), and [Carrie Steinseifer](/wiki/Carrie_Steinseifer "Carrie Steinseifer"); [Jill Sterkel](/wiki/Jill_Sterkel "Jill Sterkel") and [Mary Wayte](/wiki/Mary_Wayte "Mary Wayte") also swam in the event's second-round qualifying heat.[[12]](#cite_note-12)

For the [1988 Summer Olympics](/wiki/1988_Summer_Olympics "1988 Summer Olympics") in Seoul, South Korea, Torres qualified for the U.S. Olympic women's team in one individual event and two relay events. Torres earned a bronze medal for swimming for the third-place U.S. women's team in the [4×100-meter freestyle relay](/wiki/Swimming_at_the_1988_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women%27s_4_%C3%97_100_metre_freestyle_relay "Swimming at the 1988 Summer Olympics – Women's 4 × 100 metre freestyle relay") final, together with teammates [Mitzi Kremer](/wiki/Mitzi_Kremer "Mitzi Kremer"), [Laura Walker](/wiki/Laura_Walker_(swimmer) "Laura Walker (swimmer)"), and [Mary Wayte](/wiki/Mary_Wayte "Mary Wayte").[[11]](#cite_note-sroprofile-11)[[13]](#cite_note-13) She also earned a silver medal for swimming the freestyle leg of the [4×100-meter medley relay](/wiki/Swimming_at_the_1988_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women%27s_4_%C3%97_100_metre_medley_relay "Swimming at the 1988 Summer Olympics – Women's 4 × 100 metre medley relay") for the second-place U.S. team in the preliminary heats, but not the final.[[11]]

**Juneau** ([/ˈdʒuːnoʊ/](/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English") [ⓘ](/wiki/File:LL-Q1860_(eng)-Flame,_not_lame-Juneau,_Alaska.wav "File:LL-Q1860 (eng)-Flame, not lame-Juneau, Alaska.wav") [*JOO-noh*](/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key"); [Tlingit](/wiki/Tlingit_language "Tlingit language"): *Dzántik'i Héeni* [[ˈtsʌ́ntʰɪ̀kʼɪ̀ ˈhíːnɪ̀]](/wiki/Help:IPA "Help:IPA") transl. Base of the Flounder's River),[[6]](#cite_note-6) officially the **City and Borough of Juneau**, is the [capital](/wiki/List_of_capitals_in_the_United_States "List of capitals in the United States") of the [U.S. state](/wiki/U.S._state "U.S. state") of [Alaska](/wiki/Alaska "Alaska"), located along the [Gastineau Channel](/wiki/Gastineau_Channel "Gastineau Channel") in [Southeast Alaska](/wiki/Southeast_Alaska "Southeast Alaska"). Juneau was named the capital of Alaska in 1906, when the government of what was then the [District of Alaska](/wiki/District_of_Alaska "District of Alaska") was moved from [Sitka](/wiki/Sitka,_Alaska "Sitka, Alaska") as dictated by the [U.S. Congress](/wiki/U.S._Congress "U.S. Congress") in 1900.[[7]](#cite_note-7)[[8]](#cite_note-:0-8) On July 1, 1970, the City of Juneau merged with the City of [Douglas](/wiki/Douglas,_Alaska "Douglas, Alaska") and the surrounding Greater Juneau [Borough](/wiki/Borough_(United_States) "Borough (United States)") to form the current [consolidated city-borough](/wiki/Consolidated_city-county "Consolidated city-county"),[[9]](#cite_note-9) which ranks as the second-[largest municipality in the United States by area](/wiki/List_of_United_States_cities_by_area "List of United States cities by area") and is larger than both [Rhode Island](/wiki/Rhode_Island "Rhode Island") and [Delaware](/wiki/Delaware "Delaware").

Downtown Juneau is nestled at the base of [Mount Juneau](/wiki/Mount_Juneau "Mount Juneau") and it is across the channel from [Douglas Island](/wiki/Douglas_Island "Douglas Island"). As of the [2020 census](/wiki/2020_United_States_census "2020 United States census"), the City and Borough had a population of 32,255,[[3]](#cite_note-2020_Census_(City)

France is often referred to by the media and supporters as *Les Bleus* (The Blues), which is the nickname associated with all of France's international sporting teams due to the blue shirts each team incorporates. The team is also referred to as *Les Tricolores* or *L'Equipe Tricolore* (The Tri-color Team) due to the team's utilization of the country's national colors: blue, white, and red. During the 1980s, France earned the nickname the *"Brazilians of Europe"* mainly due to the accolades of the *"carré magique"* ("Magic Square"), who were anchored by [Michel Platini](/wiki/Michel_Platini "Michel Platini"). Led by coach [Michel Hidalgo](/wiki/Michel_Hidalgo "Michel Hidalgo"), France exhibited an inspiring, elegant, skillful and technically advanced offensive style of football, which was strikingly similar to their [South American counterparts](/wiki/Brazil_national_football_team "Brazil national football team").[[87]](#cite_note-87) Despite being offence oriented, France's defence is considered one of the best in world for their aggression and technicality. Their defence played a vital role in winning the 2018 FIFA World Cup and had earned them the title of "*Mur de fer"* ("The Iron Wall").

**Larisa Semyonovna Latynina** ([Russian](/wiki/Russian_language "Russian language"): Лариса Семёновна Латынина, née **Diriy**, Дирий; born 27 December 1934) is a Russian former [artistic gymnast](/wiki/Artistic_gymnastics "Artistic gymnastics"). Between 1956 and 1964 she won 14 [individual Olympic medals](/wiki/List_of_multiple_Olympic_medalists "List of multiple Olympic medalists") and four team medals for the [Soviet Union](/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union"). She holds the record for the most [Olympic gold medals](/wiki/Olympic_medal "Olympic medal") by a female gymnast, with nine. Her total of 18 Olympic medals was a record for 48 years. She held the record for individual event medals for over 52 years, winning 14. She is credited with helping to establish the Soviet Union as a dominant force in gymnastics.[[2]](#cite_note-2)

Kagan graduates from [Harvard Law School](/wiki/Harvard_Law_School "Harvard Law School") in 1986.

Kagan attended Hunter College High School, where her mother taught. The school had a reputation as one of the most elite learning institutions for high school girls and attracted students from all over New York City. Kagan emerged as one of the school's more outstanding students.[[17]](#cite_note-17) She was elected president of the student government and served on a student-faculty consultative committee.[[18]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGreene201425-18) Kagan then attended [Princeton University](/wiki/Princeton_University "Princeton University"), graduating in 1981 with a [Bachelor of Arts](/wiki/Bachelor_of_Arts "Bachelor of Arts"), *[summa cum laude](/wiki/Latin_honors#United_States "Latin honors")*, in history.[[19]](#cite_note-Supreme_Court-bound-19) She was particularly drawn to American history and archival research.[[20]](#cite_note-20) She wrote a senior thesis under historian [Sean Wilentz](/wiki/Sean_Wilentz "Sean Wilentz") titled "To the Final Conflict: Socialism in New York City, 1900–1933". In it she wrote, "Through its own internal feuding, then, the SP [Socialist Party] exhausted itself forever. The story is a sad but also a chastening one for those who, more than half a century after socialism's decline, still wish to change America."[[21]](#cite_note-21) Wilentz says Kagan did not mean to defend socialism, noting that she "was interested in it. To study something is not to endorse it."[[12]](#cite_note-confidence-and-canniness-12)

As an undergraduate, Kagan also served as editorial chair of *[The Daily Princetonian](/wiki/The_Daily_Princetonian "The Daily Princetonian")*.[[19]](#cite_note-Supreme_Court-bound-19)[[22]](#cite_note-22) Along with eight other students,[[a]](#cite_note-23) she penned a "Declaration of the Campaign for a Democratic University". Main article: [Sagittarius A\*](/wiki/Sagittarius_A* "Sagittarius A*")

By imaging the [Galactic Center](/wiki/Galactic_Center "Galactic Center") at [infrared](/wiki/Infrared "Infrared") wavelengths, Ghez and her colleagues have been able to peer through heavy dust that blocks visible light, to reveal images of the center of the Milky Way. Thanks to the 10-meter aperture of the [W.M. Keck Telescope](/wiki/W._M._Keck_Observatory "W. M. Keck Observatory") and the use of [adaptive optics](/wiki/Adaptive_optics "Adaptive optics") to correct for the turbulence of the atmosphere, these images of the Galactic Center are at very high spatial resolution and have made it possible to follow the orbits of stars around the black hole Sagittarius A\* (Sgr A\*). The partial orbits of many stars orbiting the black hole at the Galactic Center have been observed. One of the stars, [S2](/wiki/S2_(star) "S2 (star)"), has made a complete [elliptical orbit](/wiki/Elliptical_orbit "Elliptical orbit") since detailed observations began in 1995. Several decades more will be required to document the orbits of some of these stars completely. These measurements may provide a test of the theory of [general relativity](/wiki/General_relativity "General relativity"). In October 2012, a second star, [S0-102](/wiki/S0-102 "S0-102"), was identified by her team at UCLA, orbiting the Galactic Center.[[30]](#cite_note-30) Using [Kepler's third law](/wiki/Kepler%27s_laws_of_planetary_motion "Kepler's laws of planetary motion"), Ghez's team used the orbital motion to show that the mass of Sgr A\* is 4.1±0.6 million [solar masses](/wiki/Solar_mass "Solar mass").[[31]](#cite_note-31) Because the Galactic Center where Sgr A\* is located, is one hundred times closer than [M31](/wiki/Andromeda_Galaxy "Andromeda Galaxy") where the next nearest supermassive black hole (M31\*) is,[[32]](#cite_note-32) it is one of the best demonstrated cases for a supermassive black hole.[[33]](#cite_note-33)[[34]](#cite_note-34)

France :: Demographics :: Major cities :: chunk_0034
See also: [Functional area (France)](/wiki/Functional_area_(France) "Functional area (France)")

France is a highly urbanised country, with its [largest cities](/wiki/List_of_cities_in_France_over_20,000_population_(1999_census) "List of cities in France over 20,000 population (1999 census)") (in terms of [metropolitan area](/wiki/Functional_area_(France) "Functional area (France)") population in 2021[[242]](#cite_note-253)) being Paris (13,171,056 inh.), [Lyon](/wiki/Lyon "Lyon") (2,308,818), [Marseille](/wiki/Marseille "Marseille") (1,888,788), [Lille](/wiki/Lille "Lille") (1,521,660), [Toulouse](/wiki/Toulouse "Toulouse") (1,490,640), [Bordeaux](/wiki/Bordeaux "Bordeaux") (1,393,764), [Nantes](/wiki/Nantes "Nantes") (1,031,953), [Strasbourg](/wiki/Strasbourg "Strasbourg") (864,993), [Montpellier](/wiki/Montpellier "Montpellier") (823,120), and [Rennes](/wiki/Rennes "Rennes") (771,320). (Note: since its 2020 revision of metropolitan area borders, [INSEE](/wiki/INSEE "INSEE") considers that [Nice](/wiki/Nice "Nice") is a metropolitan area separate from the [Cannes](/wiki/Cannes "Cannes")-[Antibes](/wiki/Antibes "Antibes") metropolitan area; these two combined would have a population of 1,019,905, as of the 2021 census). [Rural flight](/wiki/Rural_flight "Rural flight") was a perennial political issue throughout most of the 20th century.
